publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Vehicle Security Systems
abstract: The author describes how, as part of the initiative against car crime, The Home Office, Police Scientific Development Branch (PSDB), is developing a security appraisal scheme for new motor cars. Its point of focus is immobilisation and its effectiveness. But because many security elements show dramatic weaknesses this appraisal scheme has been widened to include all security features and represents a whole car evaluation. It is probably the most satisfactory way to give the manufacturer an independent assessment of the thief resistance of a new car. This whole vehicle assessment strategy is broadly based: it covers the hurdles that a thief must overcome to steal the car and the resistance to theft of equipment fitted to the vehicle. Identification of the vehicle, or its parts by the police service, is also covered through vehicle identification number plates, glass etching and special markings. The first stage of a vehicle assessment is always a discussion with the manufacturer.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Vehicle anti-theft system uses radio frequency identification
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Vehicle Security Systems
abstract: Car and light van thefts are increasing alarmingly around the world and new guidelines driven by the insurance companies, are being set for vehicle manufacturers to make their products more secure. Ford has developed a new passive anti theft security system (PATS) using Texas Instruments' Registration and Identification System (TIRIS), a radio frequency technology which meets these new requirements. This new sytem is based on a tamper-proof electronic link between the driver's key and the ignition system. Each key features a tiny transponder that electronically links it to a specific vehicle. The transponder contains a unique and unalterable identification code that is accessed by radio signal from a transceiver unit in the car whenever someone tries to start the vehicle. The engine will not start unless the proper ignition key with a transponder is present, even if the ignition keylock is broken or bypassed. This method based upon radio frequency technology adds a new level of theft protection to vehicle security systems in a manner that doesn't require any effort from the drivers. In addition, this approach eliminates the normal wear and replacement of keys common to contact based security systems.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Environmental testing of electronic vehicle security systems
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Vehicle Security Systems
abstract: Environmental testing is considered to be an integral part of the evaluation of vehicle security systems in support of the Insurance Industry's Vehicle Security Scheme. Through the Scheme, launched in January 1993, MIRRC Thatcham in conjunction with the Loss Prevention Council have been testing electronic vehicle security systems throughout the year with a view to recognizing systems that perform to a defined minimum standard. This paper sets out to explain the rationale behind undertaking an environmental test programme, to detail the regime, and to report on the general findings to date.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A radar based mass movement sensor for automotive security applications
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Vehicle Security Systems
abstract: Theft of and from vehicles will be reduced by the ability to detect movement of persons within the vehicle cabin, as perimetric protection may not always be sufficient to trigger an alarm. A mass movement sensor which is reliable, robust and undetectable is required, to operate in conjunction with an effective alerting device. Whilst ultrasonic detection systems have become the technology norm for this application, they suffer from serious disadvantages in respect of false alarm rate due to their susceptibility to environmental changes when deployed within a vehicle. Here, the author describes movement sensors based on Doppler radar principles which do not exhibit false alarm behaviour and can be used in open vehicles.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Vehicle Security Systems
abstract: The author argues that in some ways there is not a lot of difference to designing before or after the production of the Thatcham rules in terms of the basic professional approach to the design function. However Thatcham is a milestone in the history of car alarm development and one can only hope that the milestone does not become a millstone or a stumbling block. So long as rules assist and do not constrain then they have a useful place to play in the scheme of things.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Paging alarm systems for automotive security applications
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Vehicle Security Systems
abstract: A busy car park in the middle of a busy town. Your attention is drawn by the sound of a car alarm siren. The source of the noise eludes you-'somewhere over there', you think to yourself looking in the general direction. You turn away and continue with your business at hand. An all too familiar circumstance where nowadays false alarms have quelled the impetus of the general public to act positively to the sound of active car alarms. Indeed greater awareness of noise pollution means that the humble car alarm is now viewed by many to be a bane of current society. The author describes how advancements in communications electronics now allows for commercially viable paging technology to be applied to the automotive security mass market. A low cost transmitter unit fitted within the vehicle communicates with a remote pager receiver to give instantaneous indications of possible intrusions.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Vehicle Security Systems
abstract: TRACKER Network (UK) Ltd has secured the agreement of all the 51 Police Forces in England, Wales and Scotland to operate the TRACKER stolen vehicle tracking and recovery system throughout Great Britain. TRACKER Network has also been granted a dedicated radio frequency by the Radio Communications Agency of the DTI and has concluded a nationwide transmission agreement with National Transcommunication Limited. In addition, type approval has been granted for all of the components of the operating system. Here, the author describes the TRACKER system which is based on a small transponder which is fitted to vehicles. When a vehicle equipped with a TRACKER unit is reported stolen, a telecommunications system linked to a central computer transmits a digitally encoded radio signal to the transponder in the stolen vehicle to activate its tracking signal. Police officers in patrol cars fitted with police tracking computers can then, in the course of normal patrol activities, detect the signal transmitted by the TRACKER unit, locate and recover the stolen vehicle.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A preliminary assessment of the risks associated with engine immobilisers
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Vehicle Security Systems
abstract: It is generally perceived that motor vehicles are easy to break into and manufacturers have been slow to provide high quality locks for doors and tailgates. Various security devices are now available either as part of the new vehicle package or as after-market accessories. There are fundamentally two types of immobiliser system, the simple mechanical lock, for example that may clamp the steering wheel to the pedals, which is intended to prevent the vehicle from being driven away, and electronic devices that may provide various means of immobilising the vehicle and can have warning alarms fitted. It is unlikely that any of these devices are thief-proof but they may slow the thief down or discourage him from selecting a particular vehicle. This paper provides a summary of a preliminary study of the factors affecting the reliability of engine immobiliser systems which was carried out for the Police Scientific Development Branch, PSDB, in February 1993.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Vehicle Security Systems
abstract: Securicor Datatrak Ltd has been involved in automatic vehicle location for over seven years, using the benefits of this technology for a variety of applications, such as resource management, the emergency services, fast response organisations as well as the security field. Here, the author describes the vehicle location and recovery system TrakBak, the brand name for a specific application offered to the private and commercial motorist, using Securicor Datatrak's existing and proven location and reporting technology.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
